passages.t: The ashes of a red heifer
passages.happening:
God gives Moses and Aaron a statute. The Israelites are to bring ‘an unblemished red heifer that has no defect and has never been placed under a yoke’ (verse 2).

It is given to Eleazar the priest, taken outside the camp and slaughtered there (verse 3). Eleazar sprinkles some of its blood seven times toward the front of the tent (verse 4). Then the whole animal is burned, ‘its hide, its flesh, and its blood’ (verse 5). The priest throws cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool onto the fire (verse 6).

A man who is clean gathers the ashes and stores them in a clean place outside the camp. “They must be kept by the congregation of Israel for preparing the water of purification” (verse 9).

Everyone who takes part, the priest, the man who burns the heifer and the man who gathers the ashes, is unclean until evening (verses 7-10).
passages.hearers:
The chapters before this one are full of death. The earth swallowed Korah's company. Fire burned 250 men. A plague killed thousands. And a whole generation has been told that it will die in the wilderness. For the next forty years, contact with the dead will be part of Israel's daily life.

In Israel's law, death was the strongest source of uncleanness. Chapter 18 answered the people's fear of coming near the sanctuary. This chapter answers the other great problem, the uncleanness that death brings on everyone who touches it. God provides a remedy that can be kept ready and used whenever it is needed.

The details are unusual. The animal is a heifer, a young cow. She must be red all over, without defect, and never used for work. Red is commonly linked with blood, the life of the animal, and the cedar and scarlet wool thrown into the fire add to the red. Hyssop was the plant ordinarily used for sprinkling in rites of cleansing.

Unlike other sacrifices, the heifer is burned whole outside the camp, blood and all. The blood, which stands for life, ends up in the ashes. Mixed later with fresh water, the ashes make a kind of stored purification offering. It can be carried to wherever a death has happened. A family does not have to go to the altar for every funeral.

Eleazar performs the rite, and not Aaron. The chapter does not say why. The likely reason is that the rite made those who performed it unclean, and the high priest had to avoid that.

The statute is for ‘the Israelites and for the foreigner residing among them’ (verse 10). Death comes to every household, and so does the remedy.
passages.later:
Hebrews notes where the heifer was killed and burned: “the bodies are burned outside the camp. And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:11-12).

The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish law compiled about AD 200, gives a whole tractate to the preparation and use of these ashes. It is called Parah, the Hebrew word for a heifer.
passages.asks: God gave Israel a remedy before the forty years of funerals began. Ask what help God has already put within your reach for a hard season that is coming or has come. And ask whether you have left it unused.

passages.happening:
“Whoever touches any dead body will be unclean for seven days” (verse 11). The same is true of anyone who is in a tent when a person dies there, and of anyone who touches a bone or a grave (verses 14-16).

The way back is simple. Some of the ashes are put in a jar and fresh water is poured over them (verse 17). A person who is clean dips hyssop in the water and sprinkles the tent, its furnishings and the people, on the third day and on the seventh. On the seventh day the person washes and bathes, ‘and that evening he will be clean’ (verse 19).

There is one warning, given twice. “But if a person who is unclean does not purify himself, he will be cut off from the assembly, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The first thing to say is that this uncleanness was not sin. It came from one of the most loving things a person can do. In Israel families washed and buried their own dead. To sit beside a dying parent, to carry a child's body to the grave, to bury a friend, all made a person unclean for seven days. The law does not blame anyone for it. It gives them a way back.

Seven days was the longest period of uncleanness for any contact in these laws. The rule is not about germs. A sealed jar in the tent stayed clean while an open one did not (verse 15). The law is making a statement about God. He is the living God, and death is the furthest thing from him. Israel's neighbors had rites that honored the dead or sought their advice. Israel's law kept death at the edge of its life before God.

The Hebrew for the ‘fresh water’ of verse 17 means living water, water that flows. Ashes that came from death are mixed with living water, and the mixture restores a person to life with God's people.

The chapter holds a puzzle. Everyone who prepares or sprinkles the water becomes unclean until evening. Yet the water makes the unclean person clean. The hard question below takes this up.

The warning is the chapter's one demand. It is not aimed at the mourner. It is aimed at the person who has a remedy freely offered and will not use it. The only one left unclean is the one who refuses to be cleansed.

The next chapter opens with the death of Miriam. The law was needed at once.
passages.later:
Hebrews draws on this chapter directly. “For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that their bodies are clean, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!” (Hebrews 9:13-14).

In the Gospels Jesus touches the dead. At Nain, “He went up and touched the coffin” of a widow's only son (Luke 7:14), and the young man sat up. Under this law the touch should have made Jesus unclean. In the Gospel, life passed from him to the dead.

David prayed in the words of this rite after his great sin: “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean” (Psalm 51:7).
passages.hard:
How can the same water make an unclean person clean and a clean person unclean?

This has puzzled readers for as long as the chapter has been read. Later Jewish teachers often treated the red heifer as the chief example of a command to be obeyed without knowing all its reasons.

Several explanations have been offered. One is that the ashes draw uncleanness to themselves, so that they take it from the unclean person, and anyone who handles them is touched by what they carry. Another is that the water is so holy that ordinary people who handle it must wash afterward, much as priests washed after handling holy things. A third is that the rite is saying how strongly death defiles, so that even its remedy leaves a mark.

The text does not choose among these. What it makes plain is the purpose. God provides a remedy for a defilement no one in Israel could avoid, and he puts it within reach of everyone, Israelite and foreigner, away from the altar.

A further word is needed, because this chapter touches on bereavement. Nothing in it says that a grieving person is at fault, or that the body of someone they love is shameful. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35).

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The only person left unclean was the one who would not be cleansed. Ask what stain you go on carrying though a remedy has been offered you: an old guilt, a grief you have told no one, a death you have never been able to speak of. And ask whom you could ask to sit with you in it.
